papers.title: AI Agents and Agentic AI in Medicine: An Autonomy-Centred Scoping Review and Research Agenda
papers.summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence agents—software systems that perceive, reason, plan and act over multiple steps with limited human intervention—are moving from research prototypes towards clinical deployment. Recent reviews map what has been built; this one asks what would have to hold for such systems to be deployed safely. We conducted a scoping review reported according to the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews, searching eight bibliographic sources from January 2017 to June 2026, admitting foundational computer science and regulatory literature alongside clinical applications. Five architectural paradigms recur—tool-augmented large language model agents, multi-agent systems, offline reinforcement learning agents, embodied robotic agents and autonomous monitoring agents—nearly all sharing a common four-layer stack. We introduce a six-level scale of clinical agent autonomy that grades systems by where human judgement enters relative to the reasoning, and by whether the resulting action remains reversible. The scale exposes an inversion in the evidence base: demonstrated patient benefit concentrates at high autonomy in narrow, bounded domains, whereas research effort concentrates at intermediate autonomy, where prospective outcome evidence is absent and automation bias is the dominant risk. papers.title: Comment and Control: Hijacking Agentic Workflows via Context-Grounded Evolution
papers.summary: Automation platforms such as GitHub Actions and n8n are increasingly adopting so-called agentic workflows, which integrate Large Language Model (LLM) agents for tasks such as code review and data synchronization. While bringing convenience for developers, this integration exposes a new risk: An adversary may control and craft certain inputs, such as GitHub issue comments, to manipulate the LLM agent for unwanted actions, such as credential exfiltration and arbitrary command execution. To our knowledge, no prior academic work has studied such a risk in agentic workflows. In this paper, we design the first detection and exploitation framework, called JAW, to hijack agentic workflows hosted on automation platforms via a novel approach called Context-Grounded Evolution. Our key idea is to evolve agentic workflow inputs under the contexts derived from hybrid program analysis for hijacking purposes. Specifically, JAW generates agentic workflow contexts through three analyses: (i) static path-feasibility analysis to identify feasible agent-invocation paths and the input constraints required to trigger them, (ii) dynamic prompt-provenance analysis to determine how that input is transformed and embedded into the LLM context, and (iii) capability analysis to identify the actions and restrictions available to the agent at runtime. papers.title: What makes an LLM a tutor? A component-centric survey of LLM-based and agentic tutoring systems
papers.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are reshaping intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) by reducing authoring costs and enabling flexible interaction. However, effective tutoring requires more than fluent responses. It also depends on pedagogical control, domain grounding, learner modeling, interaction design, orchestration, and reliable evaluation. We examine these requirements through a component-centric framework that organizes LLM-based tutoring systems into four functional layers: pedagogical policy, domain and grounding, learner state, and interaction/interface. A cross-cutting orchestration layer coordinates these components, while agentic tutoring systems are treated as an emerging subset of the broader field. Drawing on representative literature on LLM-based and agentic tutoring systems, published mostly between late 2022 and mid-2026, we analyze how tutoring capabilities are implemented across system architecture, learner modeling, interaction, orchestration, and evaluation. The reviewed literature suggests that evaluation remains concentrated on response-level and model-based proxies, while direct evidence of learning gains remains limited. Learner-state modeling and interaction design also receive less systematic attention. We conclude by identifying challenges in answer leakage, pedagogy–solving trade-offs, learner-state calibration, interaction validity, and proxy

papers.title: When to Delegate: A Measurement Study of Bounded Agent Teams for Personal Super Agents
papers.summary: Abstract Personal super agents coordinate many tools while remaining fast, safe, and accountable to one user. A popular design is a Router delegating to Workers. Recent work shows coordination can cost more than it returns, but transfer to personal agents—single-user context, side-effecting tools, cross-turn references, and refusals—is not established. We present the bounded-delegation runtime protocol, instantiate it in Eva, a 22-tool in-vehicle agent, and introduce Eva-Bench, 80 rule-scored tasks in ten categories. With one real model and tool set, we compare monolithic ReAct, bounded team, and unbounded team, and ablate budgets, reasoning, concurrency, guards, ledger, and injected failures. Delegation is not free: the main team pays 2.75×the latency and 2.59×the tokens. In one full-suite run it leads by one task (92.5% versus 91.2%), but three full-suite repetitions give 92.9% versus 93.3% (difference -0.4pp). Four post hoc temperature- matched runs average 90.6% (range 86.2–93.8%), so temperature alone does not explain the team’s small, unstable lead. We do not claim a general team advantage. The stable finding is the tax; service workflows and cross-turn references favor the team in repeated data, while safety and aggregate success do not. papers.title: Fine-Tuned Large Language Models for Theory-Aligned Social Science Content Analysis: Evidence From Collaborative Learning Discourse
papers.summary: Theory-based content analysis is central to social science research, but coding context-dependent interactional discourse remains difficult to scale. This study examines whether fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) can support theory-aligned, episode-level coding of complex social interaction, using socially shared metacognitive regulation (SSMR) in collaborative learning discourse as a demanding empirical case. Using a human-coded dataset of 2,372 discourse episodes from undergraduate collaborative problem-solving, we adapted the large language model content analysis (LACA) framework through an AI-aligned codebook, prompt design, and supervised fine-tuning. Prompt-only and fine-tuned models were compared across episode-level classification and multilayer SSMR coding. Fine-tuned models substantially improved agreement with human coding and predictive performance relative to prompt-only baselines. Performance was strongest for episode-level classification and several higher-support coding layers, whereas errors remained concentrated in sparse, boundary-prone, and highly interpretive categories requiring social-intent reconstruction and temporally unfolding context. The findings extend recent work on LLM-assisted qualitative and content analysis by showing both the promise and limits of supervised, theory-aligned automation for multilayer social interaction coding. papers.title: Delegating or Doing? Understanding User Behavior in Hybrid Human–Agent Interfaces
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded into applications, allowing users to complete tasks either through direct manipulation or by delegating actions to conversational agents. However, little is known about how users balance these modalities when both are available. We present a web-based content management system augmented with an LLM agent through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling users to perform CRUD tasks through a graphical interface, a conversational agent, or both. We conducted a between-subjects study (N=73) comparing three interaction modes: Traditional-Only, AI-First, and Hybrid. Across sixteen scenarios, we analyzed task completion time, interaction logs, and delegation behavior. AI-assisted interaction significantly reduced clicks, page navigations, and scrolling, indicating lower interaction effort. Surprisingly, these reductions did not translate into faster task completion, as task duration did not differ significantly across conditions. We also found no significant relationship between CRUD operation type and delegation, suggesting that users did not systematically avoid delegating higher-risk actions. Instead, delegation varied far more between participants than between tasks, with individual differences accounting for roughly half the variance in assistant use (ICC =.50). papers.title: SoK: Sticky Policies Come Unstuck: Where Data-Governance Claims End at Generative Handoffs
papers.summary: Modern applications move data through databases, APIs, observability pipelines, and generative systems; each hop can create a new data object: a stored derivative, an agent's tool result, per-step logs. Each component may correctly enforce its controls while the end-to-end path loses the governance basis for new outputs. LLMs both ease and complicate this crossing: they interpret ordinary-language claims without the sender's executable policy grammar, yet create content probabilistically and may release it. We characterize data-governance preservation as an architectural property of generative paths under a declared scope and trust model. At each in-scope use or release, the responsible mechanism must identify the exact output's applicable claims, join them with current request authority, and mediate every declared path. After content-changing derivation, authorized transition semantics must establish the output's governance basis and make it obtainable or resolvable downstream. We formalize this as a decision-factorization condition: correctness is possible exactly when every trusted-state equivalence class retains a common permitted decision; no universal policy language is required. We evaluate sixteen mechanism families across six lifecycle stages and four cross-stage interfaces, and we adjudicate eight product- and protocol-specific boundary paths selected as the strongest

papers.title: The Karmic cycle of reform: teacher-student interactions shaping persistent practices and pedagogical possibilities in Nepal's basic schools
papers.summary: Nepal’s school education system has seen repeated reform efforts over the past two decades, which are aiming to improve quality and equity and promote Learner-Centred Education (LCE). Yet the everyday interactions that shape teaching and learning in classrooms remain underexamined, while the classroom practices have persisted with little change over time. This persistence reflects a ‘black box’ in which policy ambitions circulate without attending to what teachers and children actually do, value, and experience in daily classroom life. This thesis explores how policy–practice gaps endure over time. It uses the locally grounded metaphor of a karmic cycle to characterise reforms that continually return in incomplete ways. To understand how pedagogical practices are enacted, experienced, and negotiated, the study positions teachers and children as central actors in shaping classroom life. Particular emphasis is placed on children’s experiences, which remain underrepresented in LCE research and Nepali policy discourse. Drawing on the theory of the pedagogical nexus and an onto-cultural perspective, the study examines how pedagogy emerges through interactions among structural pressures, cultural values, and everyday relationships. Within this nested context, culturally embedded teaching styles surfaced, forming a Nepali interpretive frame: guru (authority, discipline, responsibility

papers.title: From Hindsight to Foresight: Adapting Reusable Reasoning Structures from Recurring Financial Events
papers.summary: Forecasting real-world events requires reasoning under uncertainty from information available at a fixed cutoff. Recent work has improved how large language models (LLMs) retrieve evidence and produce probabilistic forecasts, but each question is treated independently even when similar events recur. Resolved occurrences carry experience for later forecasts, yet past outcomes and case summaries do not preserve the relationships that made an earlier occurrence informative. We develop ReFoRM (Recurrent-event Forecasting with Reasoning Memory), which organizes reasoning from resolved events into predictive paths, retrieves relevant paths for a later occurrence, and reconstructs their relations using evidence at the new forecast cutoff. We evaluate ReFoRM on the Recurring Financial Events Set, which contains 300 questions across 40 recurring financial event families and uses earlier occurrences as hindsight for 100 forecast targets. Across five LLMs and six baselines, ReFoRM improves categorical and probabilistic forecasting performance. Further analyses show that validating historical relations with current evidence and reconstructing them enhances forecasting. Reasoning evaluation also demonstrates stronger evidence grounding, logical validity, and mechanism specificity.

papers.title: SkillCODER: Towards Auditing and Attribution of Copyright Infringement in LLM Agent Skills
papers.summary: Agent skills package reusable workflows, constraints, and task-specific procedures into deployable text artifacts for LLM-based agent ecosystems. Unlike conventional system prompts, skills are distinguished by scale, spanning hundreds or thousands of tokens across many sections, and readability, being written in natural language. These properties make skills valuable but also vulnerable to copyright infringement: licensed buyers can redistribute a skill, and shared skills can be repackaged without consent. Existing copyright auditing methods for system prompts are inadequate here: skill length dilutes watermark signals, while their token-level perturbations compromise the readability essential to a skill's utility. We therefore propose SkillCODER, a method for copyright auditing and buyer attribution of agent skills under a practical black-box, content-only setting. SkillCODER operates in two phases. In the embedding phase, it parses the skill into a section-aware intermediate representation, SkillIR, that identifies stable structural anchors; it then embeds ownership evidence by distributing conditional instructions across structural nodes to form an Artifact-Gated Capsule, designed to activate under defender-designed verification queries and remain dormant otherwise; and it encodes a buyer-specific fingerprint via Controlled-Vocabulary Error-Correcting Codes that bind each co

papers.title: Llama-Polya: Instruction Tuning for Large Language Model Based on Polya’s Problem-Solving
From Learner Modeling to Human–AI Co-Regulation: A Systematic Scoping Review of Adaptive Generative AI in Personalized Learning
papers.summary: Abstract* Background Adaptive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to personalize learning, yet evidence remains fragmented across system design, human–AI co-regulation, self-regulated learning (SRL), sustained behavioral outcomes, and ethics. This systematic scoping review mapped these dimensions in a single synthesis. Methods We searched Dimensions, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, Lens, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science on 5 May 2026. Of 3,084 records identified, 95 journal articles published between 2023 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Evidence was synthesized using descriptive mapping, form–function co-occurrence analysis, and qualitative comparative synthesis. Results Adaptive GenAI was most commonly instantiated as conversational tutors, generative content personalizers, and hybrid feedback systems, with adaptive feedback, content adaptation, diagnostic analysis, scaffolding, and progress tracking emerging as the dominant functions. Conceptualizations of human–AI co-adaptation were less mature: most studies framed AI primarily as a responsive regulator, with feedback-loop acceleration and metacognitive prompting more frequently articulated than internalization, behavioral reinforcement, or social modeling. Empirical effects were concentrated in proximal SRL outcomes, particularly forethought and performance, while evidence for self-reflection, affectiv

papers.title: Digital-Twin-Driven Predictive Maintenance and Fault-Tolerant Control for Electrified Agricultural Machinery: A Multiphysics and Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for PMSM In-Wheel Drives
papers.summary: Electrified agricultural machinery increasingly relies on permanent-magnet synchronous motor drives that must remain dependable under variable traction, terrain-induced vibration, thermal cycling, contamination, and intermittent duty. Existing work offers mature methods for motor fault diagnosis, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and distributed-drive fault-tolerant control, but their health information is often not shared across diagnosis, maintenance, and control. This article develops a multiphysics digital-twin framework in which electrical, thermal, mechanical, and vibrational evidence maintains a probabilistic health belief that constrains both supervisory maintenance decisions and torque redistribution. The framework formalizes observability, uncertainty-aware health factors, deterministic safety shielding, multi-rate fallback logic, and agriculture-specific traction constraints. Reproducible low-fidelity numerical studies provide preliminary support for context-conditioned residual diagnosis and the revised thermal-continuity trade-off underlying health-aware derating, including robustness and sensitivity analyses. They do not validate sim-to-real transfer or the reinforcement-learning policy itself; those hypotheses remain open for dynamometer and hardware-in-the-loop testing. The results are therefore interpreted as mechanism-level evidence rather than field-perf

papers.title: Exploring or Exploiting Generative AI? A Dual-Path, Dual-Horizon Theory of Employee Incremental and Radical Creativity
papers.summary: Recent research has established that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is not a unitary workplace resource: exploratory and exploitative use orientations are associated with different forms of employee creativity, and their value depends on employees' capacity to integrate generated knowledge. This article therefore does not present the basic dual path as a new discovery. Instead, it develops a theoretical integration and dynamic extension that asks why the established paths operate differently, when employees should switch between them, and how short-run augmentation can evolve into either capability accumulation or capability substitution. We distinguish expansive and consolidative modes of knowledge integration, theorize phase-congruent switching rather than static ``high-high'' ambidexterity, and position metacognition as a control mechanism that governs both immediate knowledge conversion and longer-run cognitive development. We further specify cultural tightness and psychological safety as directional boundary conditions and distinguish individual creative gains from collective idea-space diversity. The framework converts emerging empirical regularities into falsifiable propositions about task phase, context, and time, providing a research agenda for sustainable human--AI creativity.

papers.title: Can TDD improve the quality of LLM-migrated code? : A pilot study in an industrial context
papers.summary: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLM) has created new possibilities for automating software development, yet ensuring the quality of AI-generated code remains a major challenge. We aim to investigate if Test-Driven Development (TDD) can improve the quality of code generated by an LLM in a fully autonomous context, within a pilot project at Decerno AB. We added TDD to their pilot workflow, using a design science approach, with continuous refinements to prompt design and workflow structure, based on observed AI behavior. The generated code was evaluated and compared with non-TDD code, using SonarQube for static code analysis. The results indicate that TDD reduced complexity and code duplication, but introduced more quality issues overall, while non-TDD produced fewer, but more severe issues. The generated tests from the TDD workflow focused more on content verification than on behavioral testing, contributing to a lower code coverage per test compared to non-TDD. The findings suggest that TDD involves trade-offs that may favor certain development priorities, in particular where lower complexity and reduced duplication are more beneficial than minimizing total issue count. This indicates that a strict application of TDD may not be optimal in an autonomous AI-driven context, and that exploring more flexible adaptations of the TDD workflow remains interesting for future resea

papers.title: From Coding to Creativity: Integrating Design Thinking into IT and Technology Education
papers.summary: This study examines how the integration of Design Thinking into Information Technology (IT) and technology education can bridge technical programming skills and creative, human-centered problem-solving. Specifically, it explores how the five stages of Design Thinking empathizing, defining, ideating, prototyping, and testing shape students’ creative thinking, active engagement, and collaborative learning experiences. A qualitative research approach was employed, involving teachers, students, and school principals as key informants. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, classroom observations, and documentation of learning activities, then analyzed thematically to identify recurring patterns in teaching practices and student experiences. The findings indicate that Design Thinking creates opportunities for students to move beyond coding procedures toward developing digital solutions that respond to real users’ needs. Through collaborative ideation, iterative prototyping, and feedback-based testing, students demonstrate greater involvement in learning, explore alternative solutions, and communicate their ideas more actively. The approach also provides opportunities to develop empathy, creativity, collaboration, and a willingness to experiment with and revise initial designs. Meanwhile, teachers assume a facilitative role by guiding inquiry, supporting experimentation, an

papers.title: Personalized to Persuade: The Effects of Contextualization and Warmth on Trust and Reliance in Conversational AI
papers.summary: Conversational agents tailor explanations to users’ backgrounds and interests, a strategy we refer to as contextualization. While personalization is an established persuasive lever in politics and marketing, its effect in everyday tasks, where users lack prior knowledge, remains unclear. We report a 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment (N = 380) testing how contextualization and conversational warmth shape the persuasiveness of, and reliance on, an AI assistant that argues against expert recommendations. Contextualization and warmth each reduce persuasiveness, yet their combination restores it through a crossover interaction. Behavioral reliance is high in every condition and invariant to conversational design. Trust predicts both outcomes but mediates neither. AI literacy decouples attitude from behavior: more literate users report lower trust, yet are more persuaded and more likely to abandon the expert position.

papers.title: Where Does the Human End? Creative Agency with Generative AI across Five Years of Chinese Digital Painting
papers.summary: As generative AI enters creative work, practitioners must decide where AI assistance ends and human authorship begins. Human-agent interaction (HAI) research has examined AI as a tool, collaborator, consultant, and competitor. The longitudinal problem is how these roles are revised as systems become more capable, public, and economically embedded. We report a five-year interview study with 17 Chinese digital painters, based on annual semi-structured interviews from 2021 to 2025. Participants described recurring but non-uniform patterns of protective resistance, pragmatic task delegation, and, for some, reflective agency repartitioning. Early resistance protected observation, originality, signature, and ownership from AI. Later delegation placed AI in bounded tasks such as references, backgrounds, rough sketches, and client-facing drafts. By 2025, some participants built hybrid workflows around human-only zones, while others described fatigue, precarity, or difficulty locating a remaining human role. Peer norms, emotional climates, and production pressures shaped which delegations felt useful, acceptable, or exhausting. Copyright, authorship, and creative labor remained recurring limits on what participants were willing to delegate. We frame these accounts as longitudinal agency partitioning, the situated work of deciding which stages, responsibilities, values, and claims remain

papers.title: Reasoning More, Knowing No Better? Epistemic Calibration in Financial Reasoning Tasks
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) reportedly 'reason' with increasing sophistication, but whether they 'know' when they are wrong remains poorly understood. We study epistemic calibration, the alignment between expressed confidence and empirical correctness, across approximately 30 contemporary models and configurable reasoning-effort budgets, using XFinBench (graduate-level financial reasoning) and SQuAD v2 (answerable and unanswerable questions). Reported confidence stays high relative to accuracy, with weak discrimination between correct and incorrect or unsupported answers. Miscalibration follows a Dunning-Kruger-like pattern: weaker models are often strongly overconfident, while frontier models are mildly underconfident. Reasoning effort significantly improves accuracy but has no detectable effect on the confidence-accuracy gap or ECE; stable between-model differences explain over 96% of calibration variance, versus a negligible effort effect. Calibration deteriorates most on scenario planning and numerical modeling. On SQuAD v2, models answer four in five unanswerable questions and remain near-maximally confident even when no answer is supported; higher reasoning effort yields no robust gain in calibration or abstention after multiplicity correction. We discuss implications for evaluation, deployment, and the design of calibration-aware, boundary-aware financial reasoning syst

papers.title: TurboRetry: Mitigating Large-Scale QUIC Handshake Floods with Off-the-Shelf DPU Offloading
papers.summary: The modern transport protocol QUIC is designed to enhance network performance and security, but it remains vulnerable to handshake flooding attacks. Such attacks exhaust CPU resources by forcing the server to perform expensive cryptographic operations via a large number of handshaking requests. QUIC provides a built-in defense mechanism, the Retry mechanism, to mitigate these attacks. However, our experiments reveal that it can still become a performance bottleneck under large-scale QUIC handshake floods due to substantial computational overhead. In this paper, we design and implement TurboRetry, a split design, that offloads the Retry mechanism onto DPUs to efficiently mitigate QUIC handshake floods. TurboRetry partitions the tasks of the Retry into two categories, and then assigns them to the DPUs and the host, respectively. To preserve QUIC semantics and reduce the coordination overhead, TurboRetry designs an extended Retry token format and an efficient cooperation scheme. In addition, TurboRetry offloads the connection authorization task to the on-path Data Path Accelerator (DPA) to further improve both performance and security. Our evaluation shows that TurboRetry increases the maximum sustainable attack rate by 10--20× over host QUIC stacks.

papers.title: Investigating the association between problematic social media use and the feeling of self-alienation.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: Transformations, Empirical Evidence and Challenges for Student-Centred University Learning
papers.summary: The rapid evolution and integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, particularly following the advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Generative AI (GenAI), have profoundly transformed teaching, learning and management practices in higher education worldwide. This paper aims to synthesise the empirical evidence available between 2020 and 2026 regarding the impact of AI in higher education, examining the prevalent technologies, pedagogical mediation, levels of human–AI collaboration, adoption patterns and ethical-normative implications. A systematic literature review was conducted in rigorous accordance with the PRISMA 2020 Statement. Six international scientific databases were consulted: Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, SciELO, PubMed and IEEE Xplore, identifying an initial corpus of 1,247 records. After the screening process for duplicates, title/abstract and full-text reading, 45 primary studies focused on university educational impact were selected, analytically complemented by global bibliometric and meta-systematic reviews of the period. Methodological quality was assessed using the MMAT (2018) tool and the certainty of the evidence via the GRADE approach. It is concluded that the predominant AI technologies in the literature are large language models (75.6 %), intelligent tutoring systems (31.1 %) and learning analytics tools (24.4 %). papers.title: Video and digital games: Historical controversies, benefits, and risks for children and adolescents
papers.summary: Video and digital games have been the focus of sustained public and scientific debate since their commercial emergence in the late 1970s, particularly regarding their effects on children and adolescents. Early public and scientific discourse frequently portrayed gaming as a source of physical injury, addiction, aggression, social isolation, academic problems, and moral decline. However, subsequent empirical research has produced a substantially more differentiated picture of both the benefits and risks of gaming. This review examines the historical foundations of controversies surrounding video and digital games and synthesizes contemporary evidence concerning their cognitive, emotional, social, therapeutic, and physical effects. . Research indicates that moderate, purposeful gaming may improve visuospatial abilities, attentional control, problem-solving, mood regulation, social connection, and selected educational outcomes. Gaming-based interventions have also demonstrated therapeutic potential, particularly for depressive symptoms and attention-related difficulties among young people. At the same time, important risks remain, especially when gaming becomes excessive, compulsive, or disruptive to everyday functioning. These include repetitive-strain injuries, sleep disruption, problematic gaming, and adverse mental-health and academic outcomes. Evidence concerning violent game

papers.title: An Assessment of Accessibility and Affordability of Inpatient Psychiatric Care in Tennessee
papers.summary: Introduction: Access to mental health has seen changes over the past decade, but little research and attention have been given to access to inpatient psychiatric facilities. Inpatient psychiatric care is crucial for patients experiencing mental health emergencies who need immediate access to care. Gaps in spatial accessibility, affordability, and the access and assessment process were identified due to a lack of available information in the field. Methods: Secondary data from the Tennessee Department of Health were used to assess financial accessibility through payer source charges and patient encounters, as well as through mapping of inpatient psychiatric facilities and conducting drive time and coverage area analyses. Primary data were collected through interviews with clinicians located in Northeastern Tennessee to gain insight into the assessment process and gather their perceptions of inpatient care. Results: Longitudinal descriptive reviews on the financial accessibility among Tennessee Inpatient Facilities. This showed increased variability among facilities when stratified by region, ownership, and type of operation. Spatial accessibility in ArcGIS showed 82% of counties were not covered within a 30-minute radius of inpatient facilities. Analysis showed that Middle Tennessee had significantly less coverage from inpatient facilities and raised concerns about spatial-socia

papers.title: Pieces Solving a Puzzle: Emerging Roles and Cross-Field Analogies During a Distributed Epistemic Game
papers.summary: In an effort to describe why some problems can’t be solved, a character compared them to a cubic meter of platinum - a block so dense that all the people who could squeeze around it still couldn’t lift it off the ground. In the same way, these problems simply can’t have enough people gathered around and communicating about them - and so they remain unsolved. This research looks at the first Polymath Project (2009) as an example of a distributed epistemic game to examine how groups engage with complex problems. and without a locally omniscient individual. In this setting of epistemic uncertainty, interactions between individuals reveal patterns of participation, and an analogy opens a new solution pathway by introducing a problem-solving approach from another field. These insights answer the initial question of the Polymath Project - ‘Is massively collaborative mathematics possible?’ - and offer hope for lifting the cubic meter of other unsolvable problems.

papers.title: Sex-Dependent Modulation of the Endocannabinoid System in Pain Processing
papers.summary: Medical cannabis, also known as medical marijuana, is becoming a more popular treatment for many diseases, including chronic pain. Chronic pain is difficult to treat, and current pain relievers are less effective in women. Medical cannabis may be a useful alternative to the medications that are currently available, but more research is needed to determine how safe and effective it is. Cannabis belongs to a class of drugs known as cannabinoids, which act on the body’s own endocannabinoid system to produce its effects. Cannabinoids affect the sexes differently, but it is not clear what causes these differences. Our research explored how sex hormones like estrogen and testosterone affect the efficacy of cannabinoids. To do this, I first examined whether removing these hormones would affect the brain’s response to THC, the main ingredient in cannabis. I found that THC affected brain regions differently in mice with depleted hormones. Additionally, THC affected brain regions differently in males and females. Next, I tested whether testosterone and estrogen affected how well cannabinoids worked as pain relievers. I found that testosterone reduced the drug’s efficacy in females, while estrogens reduced its efficacy in males. This would suggest that hormones have a different effect on males and females, leading to differences in the cannabinoid’s pain-relieving ability. Lastly, I sough

papers.title: Digital twins for intelligent intersections: A literature review
papers.summary: Intelligent intersections play a pivotal role in urban mobility, demanding innovative solutions such as digital twins to enhance safety and efficiency. This literature review investigates the integration and application of digital twins for intelligent intersections, a critical area within smart urban traffic systems. The review systematically categorizes existing research into five key thematic areas: (i) Digital Twin Architectures and Frameworks; (ii) Data Processing and Simulation Techniques; (iii) Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Adaptive Traffic Control; (iv) Safety and Protection of Vulnerable Road Users; and (v) Scaling from Localized Intersections to Citywide Traffic Networks. Each theme is explored comprehensively, highlighting significant advancements, current challenges, and critical insights. The findings reveal that multi-layered digital twin architectures incorporating real-time data fusion and AI-driven decision-making enhances traffic efficiency and safety. Advanced simulation techniques combined with sophisticated AI/ML algorithms demonstrate notable improvements in real-time responsiveness and predictive accuracy for traffic management. Additionally, the integration of digital twins has shown substantial promise in safeguarding vulnerable road users through proactive and adaptive safety strategies. papers.title: Between the Lines: Multi-turn Contextual Investment Advice Detection
papers.summary: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly power financial conversational assistants, detecting investment advice in natural language has become a critical regulatory and safety challenge. Unlike explicit single-turn recommendations, investment advice often emerges implicitly and progressively over multi-turn conversations, shaped by user intent, delivery style, and contextual buildup. We introduce the first comprehensive framework for detecting both sequential and contextual investment advice in dialogue settings. Central to our approach is a modular, top-down synthetic data generation pipeline that systematically spans a taxonomy of advisory trajectories using an axis-bucket-descriptor schema. We simulate both benign and high-risk conversations across diverse user personas, financial instruments, and risk tiers, and evaluate detection capabilities using LLM-as-a-Judge with entropy-based uncertainty diagnostics. Our results show that contextual advisory detection remains substantially more challenging than sequential cases, even under few-shot prompting with tailored demonstrations. This work lays the foundation for scalable guardrail development in highstakes, compliance-sensitive domains, where advisory risk is often subtle, distributed, and perception-dependent.
